bottleneck: Brain and other organoids grow without blood vessels, so cells in the interior starve and die once the structure exceeds diffusion limits of a few millimeters. Without vasculature, organoids cannot mature into truly functional tissue, model adult physiology, or serve as transplantable grafts. Vascularization in a dish requires co-developing endothelial networks that actually perfuse — a problem as hard as organogenesis itself — and simply adding endothelial cells produces disorganized, non-functional tubes.
current_state: Co-culture with endothelial cells and microfluidic perfusion produce primitive vessels, but no organoid yet has a functional, hierarchical vasculature capable of sustaining mature tissue.

sources.title: Architecting the Future of Health: From Code to Cure

title: Organoids die from the inside without vasculature
why_it_blocks: Vascularization is the gate between organoids as disease models and organs as replacements. Until vessels grow with tissue, lab-grown organs remain science demonstrations, not transplants, and the organ shortage continues unabated.
